title: Irish Traditional Music — Overview
snippet: Irish Traditional Music — Overview Irish Traditional Music — Overview **Track:** regions | **Tier:** 1 | **Difficulty:** 3/10 **Prerequisites:** theory-scales-major-intro **Tags:** ireland, celtic, tradition, session, overview, gaeltacht, fleadh Overview Walk into a pub in Ennis
text: Irish Traditional Music — Overview Irish Traditional Music — Overview **Track:** regions | **Tier:** 1 | **Difficulty:** 3/10 **Prerequisites:** theory-scales-major-intro **Tags:** ireland, celtic, tradition, session, overview, gaeltacht, fleadh Overview Walk into a pub in Ennis on a Thursday night and you may hear three fiddles, a flute, a box accordion, and a bodhrán negotiating the turn from *The Silver Spear* into *The Musical Priest* without a word spoken. Walk into a hall in Mullingar in August and you may hear the same tune played by a fifteen-year-old who has practised it for months to meet adjudicators' standards. Both scenes are Irish traditional music. Both are "trad." Neither is more authentic than the other — but they answer different social needs, and a musician who understands only one will miss half the picture. This lesson is your map. Before you study instruments, tune forms, dance, or the long history of collectors and 78 rpm records, you need orientation: what people mean by *trad* versus *Celtic*, where the music lives, what the main tune types feel like, how songs sit alongside dance music, and which institutions keep the tradition moving. Think of it as arriving in a new city with a good guidebook rather than a single street address. Irish traditional music is a living oral tradition of dance tunes, songs, and instrumental style. Wikipedia's *Music of Ireland* article stresses that despite emigration and mass exposure to British and American pop, Ireland's indigenous music **remained vibrant through the 20th century and into the 21st** — and in turn influenced country and roots music in the United States, which later fed back into rock. Fusion is not a betrayal of tradition; it is part of the story you will trace through this unit. "Trad" versus "Celtic": labels that help and mislead **Irish traditional music** (*ceol traidisiúnta na hÉireann*) usually means orally transmitted dance music and song in Irish or English, played on acoustic instruments associated with the island: fiddle, flute, whistle, uilleann pipes, harp, button accordion, concertina, bodhrán, and others. Players learn tunes by ear, share **sets** at gatherings, and ornament melodies with cuts, rolls, bowed triplets, and tongued articulation. Written scores, tune books, and databases exist — Francis O'Neill's *Music of Ireland*, Brendan Breathnach's *Ceol Rince na hÉireann*, websites like *The Session* — but they supplement listening and copying living players; they do not replace them. **Celtic music** is a broader umbrella. Wikipedia describes it as a grouping of folk genres that evolved from the traditions of Celtic peoples across Northwestern Europe — Ireland, Scotland, Wales, Brittany, Galicia, and related diasporas. It covers both orally transmitted music and recorded hybrids, from pure session repertoire to festival stages where Rapalje-style bands blend pipes with rock staging. Irish trad is one branch of that family, often the best known abroad, but it is not interchangeable with "Celtic." A Breton *gavotte*, a Galician *muiñeira*, and a Sligo reel share historical cousins; they do not share identical rhythm, ornament, or social context. Marketing has blurred the line. Gift shops sell "Celtic meditation" albums that have little to do with a Clare session. Conversely, some purists reject anything labelled Celtic as tourist kitsch — which dismisses legitimate cross-regional collaboration. As a student, hold two ideas at once: **Irish trad** names a specific island tradition with its tune types and session culture; **Celtic** names a wider network of related styles. When you choose recordings, prefer specificity ("East Galway fiddle," "Donegal highlands") over a generic shamrock template. ![Celtic fusion band performing at a festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Keltfest_2010_%284610513447%29.jpg?width=640) The Gaeltacht and the oral tradition The **Gaeltacht** (*Gaeltachtaí* in plural) denotes regions where Irish remains a community language — parts of Connemara, the Aran Islands, Donegal's west, Kerry's Dingle peninsula, and other pockets. Traditional music and Gaeltacht life overlap but are not the same thing. Plenty of world-class trad musicians grew up in English-speaking Dublin, Belfast, or Chicago; plenty of Gaeltacht communities face the same global pop pressures as anywhere else. Still, the Gaeltacht matters for **sean-nós song** (*amhránaíocht ar an sean-nós* — "old-style singing"), where Irish-language poetry, local dialect, and personal phrasing survive in unaccompanied performance. **Oral transmission** means the tune passes person to person: at a kitchen table, a summer-school class, a pub session, a feis waiting room. The melody may shift — a extra turn in the B part, a different name, a new key to suit a whistle. That variation is a feature, not a bug. Print and recording freeze moments in time; the living tradition keeps moving. When Michael Coleman recorded *The Boys of the Lough* in New York in 1921, he fixed one version that became "standard" for generations — yet session players still vary it nightly. Oral tradition does not mean anti-technology. Modern learners use slow-down apps, YouTube, and ABC files. The question is whether you treat those tools as the **source** or as a **teacher** pointing you back toward players. Competitions, archives, and radio also transmit music — Comhaltas classes, RTÉ programmes, the Irish Traditional Music Archive (ITMA) in Dublin. Healthy tradition uses all channels; unhealthy tradition either rejects the past entirely or fossilises one collector's edition as holy writ. Comhaltas Ceoltóirí Éireann runs classes and branches worldwide; Irish Traditional Music Archive preserves recordings and manuscripts; the Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann gathers competitors and audiences each summer. The session (*seisiún*) A **session** is an informal gathering where musicians play tunes in **sets** — usually two or three tunes of the same form before switching. The word *seisiún* as a label for these gatherings is relatively recent (Wikipedia notes it was "invented in the 1990s" in some Irish circles), but the practice is old: neighbours with fiddles and flutes playing for dancers and listeners. ![A traditional music session](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Dungloe_music_festival_%281%29_-_geograph.org.uk_-_51567.jpg?width=640) Sessions happen in pubs, festival tents, summer-school corridors, and private homes. They are social contracts. Unwritten rules vary by room, but the following will serve you almost anywhere: **Listen before you join.** Arrive early, buy a drink if you're in a pub, stand where you can hear, and count how many tunes make a set before anyone switches form. Jumping in mid-tune or mid-set disrupts the room. Regulars notice newcomers who respect the music; they also notice newcomers who treat the session as a backing track for their solo. Humility is not weakness — it is how you earn the nod to start the next set. **Know when not to play.** If the room is packed with melody players and someone is already struggling to be heard, adding another fiddle may help nobody. Some sessions designate a rotation; others rely on eye contact. When in doubt, play quietly or lay out for a tune and learn the local repertoire for next time. **Match tempo and volume.** Faster is not better. If the room is playing at a comfortable dance tempo, do not accelerate to show off. Uilleann pipes and harp suit smaller spaces; fiddle, flute, and accordion can dominate acoustically — balance matters. **Respect the form.** Do not drop a slow air into a reel set without warning. Do not switch from jigs to polkas until the set ends. Tunes of the same metre chain together; crossing metres feels like changing gears without a clutch. **Keys:** D major, G major, A major, and E minor cover a large share of session repertoire. title: Irish Instruments — Traditional Voices I
snippet: Irish Instruments — Traditional Voices I Irish Instruments — Traditional Voices I **Track:** regions | **Tier:** 2 | **Difficulty:** 4/10 **Prerequisites:** regions-celtic-ireland-01-overview **Tags:** ireland, fiddle, flute, whistle, pipes, harp, regional-style, session Overview
text: Irish Instruments — Traditional Voices I Irish Instruments — Traditional Voices I **Track:** regions | **Tier:** 2 | **Difficulty:** 4/10 **Prerequisites:** regions-celtic-ireland-01-overview **Tags:** ireland, fiddle, flute, whistle, pipes, harp, regional-style, session Overview This lesson examines five instruments at the heart of Irish traditional music: the **fiddle**, **flute**, **tin whistle**, **uilleann pipes**, and **Celtic harp** (*cláirseach*). Guidebooks and festival programmes often group them as "melody instruments" — a shorthand that helps beginners find the tune line in a noisy pub, but a misleading map if you treat it as law. A fiddle bow can drive rhythm like a drum; uilleann pipes play chordal **regulators** behind the chanter; a harpist may harmonise a song or step into the tune line in a small ensemble. Session culture rewards **listening** over labelling: the same player may lead one set, drop to accompaniment the next, and sit out a tune in a key they do not know. The five voices share a family resemblance — diatonic tune types in D, G, A, and related modes; ornament built from cuts, rolls, and articulation rather than romantic vibrato; repertoire learned by ear from recordings, classes, and nights in kitchens. They differ in breath versus bow, in indoor versus outdoor volume, and in regional accent. A Sligo fiddle roll is not a Donegal snap; a Clare flute player may phrase differently from a Dublin whistle prodigy. This lesson gives you enough detail to recognise each instrument, name major stylists, and understand how geography and history shaped sound. Read it alongside **Session Voices II**, which covers bodhrán, guitar, accordion, banjo, and other voices that equally refuse a single "rhythm only" or "melody only" slot. Session roles overlap Before diving into each instrument, clear away the most common beginner mistake: sorting the session into a melody column and a rhythm column. Real sessions are messier and more interesting. | Situation | What you might hear | |-----------|---------------------| | Reel in a full pub | Fiddle and flute on the tune, banjo doubling an octave up, guitar outlining chords, bodhrán marking lift — but the accordion may have **started** the set with the melody | | Slow air | Uilleann pipes or fiddle alone; harp adding bass-hand damping; whistle player silent because the key or mood does not suit | | House session | Pipes with regulators providing **harmony**; flute resting; harp accompanying song | | Competition stage | Whistle player performing a virtuoso hornpipe while no "rhythm section" plays at all | **Overlap in practice:** - **Fiddle** — Usually leads, but also supplies rhythmic bow lift, drones on open strings, and harmony in twin-fiddle regions. - **Flute and whistle** — Lead in most keys; can harmonise each other in thirds; whistle often taught first but played at master level for life. - **Uilleann pipes** — Chanter melody plus regulator chords; piper may be the only sounding instrument on an air. - **Harp** — Concert and song settings; can play tune lines in smaller rooms; not typical as the loudest voice in a crowded bar. The next lesson covers guitar, bouzouki, bodhrán, accordion, and banjo — equally capable of leading, supporting, or sitting out. **Who starts the tune** and **who matches whose phrasing** matter more than any chart. ![Session musicians with bodhrán at a gathering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/177-Bodhran-Hinnerk-Ruemenapf-0037-p70.jpg?width=640) --- Irish fiddle The **Irish fiddle** is the violin played with traditional bowing, ornamentation, and intonation habits. Richard Head's 1674 account of Sunday life in Ireland — "in every field a fiddle, and the lasses footing until they foam up" — shows how deeply the instrument was tied to dance before concert stages or recording studios existed. Dublin maker **Thomas Perry** (c. 1744–1818) and others mass-produced violins on English models, putting affordable instruments into rural hands. Emigration carried fiddlers to London, New York, and Chicago; **78 rpm records** sent styles back across the Atlantic so that a Sligo accent heard in County Mayo might have been learned from a New York pressing. Technique, posture, and ornament Irish fiddlers typically hold the instrument in standard violin posture — chin on rest, left hand on the neck — but the **sound and articulation** diverge sharply from classical training. **Vibrato** is used sparingly, most often on slow airs; dance tunes rely on **cuts** (a quick grace note above the main pitch), **rolls** (ornament patterns around a sustained note), **trebles** (bowed triplets), and **slides** into target notes. Bowing carries regional identity: **slurs into the beat** on reels create lift; Donegal players use **stronger detaché** and bow pressure; Clare players may favour a slightly looser, loping pulse on polkas and slides. Open strings ring as **drone** colour — especially G and D in fiddle-friendly keys. Tunings are standard G-D-A-E unless a player experiments with scordatura for a particular tune (uncommon but not unknown in older regional practice). Many players learn by ear at kitchen sessions; written scores from O'Neill's *Music of Ireland* or online ABC files are references, not substitutes for listening to phrasing. Session and band role In most pub sessions the fiddle is a **default leader**: repertoire breadth, volume, and social prestige keep it central. That does not mean it always plays the top line. Two fiddlers may play in **unison** or **harmony** (Donegal and Scottish-border traditions emphasise twin fiddling). In bands from Ceoltóirí Chualann to Altan, fiddle shares leadership with flute, accordion, or pipes depending on arrangement. A sensitive session fiddler **drops volume** when pipes or a solo flute take an air, and **matches ornament** rather than inventing a competing layer. Regional schools: Donegal, Sligo, and Clare Irish fiddle style is not one accent. Three regions dominate discussion — each with sub-local flavours. **Sligo** style is fast, flamboyant, and roll-heavy. Bowing is fluid; fingered rolls decorate reel and jig lines densely. The county's diaspora recordings made Sligo synonymous with "Irish fiddle" abroad for much of the twentieth century. Repertoire overlaps with neighbouring Leitrim and Roscommon; session players worldwide still default to Sligo-settings of standards like or . **Donegal** fiddling bears **Scottish influence** — marches, strathspeys, and highlands appear beside reels and jigs. Bowing is **assertive**; short bow strokes and **trebles** cut through. The **travelling fiddler** tradition — players moving between fairs and houses with vast tune memory — is epitomised by **John Doherty** (1900–1980), from Ardara. Donegal also produced **Tommy Peoples** (1945–2018), whose fierce ornamentation and precision influenced generations after he settled in Clare. **Clare** is often described as a **session county** rather than a single fiddle "accent": fiddle sits alongside strong concertina and accordion traditions. **Martin Hayes** (born 1961, East Clare) represents a lyrical, sometimes **rubato** approach — long bow strokes, emotional slow airs, and reel phrasing that prioritises **feel** over flash. Clare sessions may be less uniformly fast than Sligo stereotypes suggest; listening to local players beats importing a generic template. **Sliabh Luachra** (Cork–Kerry border) deserves mention: polkas, slides, and local tune names; fiddle bowing adapts to 2/4 and 12/8 forms. **East Galway** and **West Cork** have their own favoured players and tune stock. | Region | Bowing / ornament | Repertoire notes | |--------|-------------------|------------------| | Sligo | Heavy rolls, smooth slurs | Diaspora 78s defined global expectations | | Donegal | Strong bow, trebles, Scottish forms | Marches, highlands, travelling tradition | | Clare | Lyrical to driving depending on player | Session mix with box and concertina | |

title: Irish Instruments — Session Voices II
snippet: Irish Instruments — Session Voices II Irish Instruments — Session Voices II **Track:** regions | **Tier:** 3 | **Difficulty:** 5/10 **Prerequisites:** regions-celtic-ireland-02-instruments-voices-i **Tags:** ireland, bodhrán, guitar, bouzouki, banjo, mandolin, concertina, accordi
text: Irish Instruments — Session Voices II Irish Instruments — Session Voices II **Track:** regions | **Tier:** 3 | **Difficulty:** 5/10 **Prerequisites:** regions-celtic-ireland-02-instruments-voices-i **Tags:** ireland, bodhrán, guitar, bouzouki, banjo, mandolin, concertina, accordion, harmonica, session-roles Overview This lesson covers instruments that entered Irish sessions across different centuries — **bodhrán**, **bones**, **guitar**, **bouzouki**, **mandolin**, **tenor banjo**, **concertina**, **button accordion**, and **harmonica**. Some are indigenous or long-rooted (frame drum, bones); others arrived through **diaspora**, **jazz age**, or **1960s–70s fusion** (guitar, bouzouki, banjo in trad lineup). All are now part of the soundscape from Miltown Malbay to Melbourne. The organising mistake to avoid is sorting them into rigid **"rhythm"** and **"melody"** columns. In Clare, the button accordion often **leads** the tune. Tenor banjo **doubles** fiddle melody an octave up while adding percussive attack. Guitar supplies harmony but may introduce **counter-melody**. Bodhrán marks pulse — yet overplaying turns it into a **tempo dictator**, the most common session faux pas. Concertina and accordion share **bellows and free reeds** but occupy different regional niches. Good musicianship means **listening** and **role flexibility**, not permanent labels. Read **Traditional Voices I** for fiddle, flute, whistle, pipes, and harp. Together, the two lessons map a typical pub ensemble without pretending every county sounds the same. Session roles overlap Sessions are **social contracts**. Instruments negotiate leadership tune by tune — not by category. | Instrument | Can lead melody | Can accompany | Session reality | |------------|-----------------|---------------|-----------------| | Button accordion | Yes — especially Clare/Kerry | Yes — bass chords used sparingly | Often **starts** sets in Munster pubs | | Anglo concertina | Yes | Yes — harmonic pads possible | Strong in Clare, West Limerick, some English-Irish crossover | | Tenor banjo | Yes — doubles fiddle line | Percussive drive on off-beats | Cuts through noise; Dubliners legacy | | Mandolin | Counter-melody, chops | Chord chops on off-beats | Bluegrass-adjacent technique, Irish repertoire | | Guitar | Rarely sole lead | Yes — DADGAD, capo, picking | Latecomer now **standard** | | Bouzouki | Counter-melody lines | Open-chord accompaniment | Planxty-era innovation | | Bodhrán | No | Pulse and colour | **One per session** often enough | | Bones | No | Click rhythm | Portable; ties to lilting | | Harmonica | Fills, melody | Blues inflection | Not core everywhere | **Overlap examples:** - **Accordion and concertina** both use bellows; either may play **unison melody** with fiddle or **rest** during song. - **Banjo and mandolin** share plectrum attack; banjo often **octaves fiddle** while mandolin **chops** chords. - **Guitar and bouzouki** both supply harmony; bouzouki **rings longer** on open strings; guitar **caps** for key change. - **Bodhrán** should **follow** melody phrasing — if it leads, the session feels like a drum circle, not trad. **Who starts the tune?** Watch that, not the instrument chart. ![Holy Cross Accordion Band at Fleadh Cheoil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/IMG_E9670_Holy_Cross_Accordion_Band_Atticall.jpg?width=640) --- Bodhrán The **bodhrán** (pronounced roughly BO-rawn) is a **single-headed frame drum**, typically 35–45 cm in diameter, with a wooden rim and goatskin or synthetic head. The player strikes with a **tipper** (*cipín* — a short beater, straight or curved) and alters tone by pressing the **non-striking hand** inside the skin against the rim. Wikipedia and ethnomusicologists debate whether the bodhrán is **ancient** or largely a **nineteenth-century southwest Irish** development; either way, its **session prominence** exploded in the **twentieth-century revival**, especially after ensemble experiments legitimised frame drum in trad bands. Technique, posture, and ornament The player usually sits, drum held **vertically** on the knee or angled inward. **Tipper technique** varies: **Kerry style** may use rapid wrist strokes; **West Limerick** players favour **smoother ride** patterns; some use **double-ended tippers** for roll effects. The **inside hand** is the secret: pressing toward the rim **raises pitch** and dampens overtones; a light touch leaves the skin **boomy**; a firm press yields **dry, tight** clicks. Good bodhrán playing **mirrors melody phrasing** — accenting reel lift on beats two and four, jig pulse in groups of three — rather than metronomic thumping. **Ornament** on bodhrán means **timbral variation**: sliding the inside hand while striking, **rim shots**, or **pausing** during tune transitions. Less is often more. Session and band role Bodhrán supplies **pulse and colour**. It should **enter after** melody establishes tempo — experienced players **listen** before striking. In bands (**The Chieftains**, **De Dannan**, **Lúnasa**), bodhrán adds **drive** without replacing fiddle rhythm. In sessions, **one bodhrán** is a common etiquette rule; two uncordinated drums **fight** the tune. **Seán Ó Riada** (1931–1971) placed bodhrán in **Ceoltóirí Chualann** arrangements — controversial then, influential forever. Ó Riada treated Irish ensemble as **orchestration**, not accidental pub volume; bodhrán gained **legitimacy** beside harp, pipes, and fiddle on stage. **Memorable detail:** Before Ó Riada, some trad purists saw bodhrán as **inferior or modern**; after Ceoltóirí Chualann and **The Chieftains**, it became **iconic**. Notable players: **Mel Mercier**, **Colm Murphy**, **John Joe Kelly** (Lúnasa) — each with distinct **touch** (Mercier's Clare sensitivity, Kelly's athletic drive). **Ronan Ó Snodaigh** (Kíla) experiments with **multicultural** frame-drum vocabulary while rooted in Irish pulse — reminder that bodhrán technique continues to evolve beyond revival orthodoxy. Manufacturing and maintenance Modern bodhráns often feature **mechanical tuners** around the rim — players adjust head tension for humidity and room temperature. **Goatskin** heads respond to weather; **synthetic** heads stabilise touring conditions. **Tippers** range from **hot-rod** thin (bright attack) to **bulb** ends (softer thump). Beginners obsess over drum diameter; teachers insist **inside-hand** skill matters more than brand. Regional associations Bodhrán appears **nationwide** in revival sessions; **Kerry**, **Clare**, and **West Limerick** claim strong teaching lineages. **Miltown Malbay** summer school courses include bodhrán alongside pipes and fiddle. Manufacture thrives — **Paraic McNeela**, **Seamus O'Kane**, and other makers serve global demand. Historical notes Older museum examples sometimes show **scarf-joined wooden frames** — pre-industrial workshop construction. Mid-twentieth-century **revival** transformed bodhrán from occasional folk prop to **session default**. Critique persists: **over-loud bodhrán** remains the cliché session complaint. The instrument rewards **restraint**. ![Bodhrán frame drum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Bodhran.jpg?width=640) ![Bodhrán player using tipper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Bodhran_player.jpg?width=640) --- Bones **Bones** are paired **sticks** — wood, bone, or synthetic — held in one hand and clicked rhythmically. They are **idiophones**: the sound is the material itself, not a membrane or string. Irish and **Appalachian** traditions share bones ancestry; **African-American** bones virtuosity influenced American folk percussion. In Ireland, bones accompany **house dance**, **lilting**, and pub sessions where a drummer is absent. Technique and cultural context The player curls fingers around one stick; the second stick **strikes** it with wrist rotation — fast **triplets** and reel pulse possible at expert level. Bones are **loud** for their size — portable rhythm for kitc

title: Tunes, Forms, and Style
snippet: Tunes, Forms, and Style Tunes, Forms, and Style **Track:** regions | **Tier:** 4 | **Difficulty:** 4/10 **Prerequisites:** regions-celtic-ireland-03-instruments-voices-ii **Tags:** ireland, jig, reel, hornpipe, polka, slide, ornamentation, sean-nós, ballad, slow-air, lilting, ses
text: Tunes, Forms, and Style Tunes, Forms, and Style **Track:** regions | **Tier:** 4 | **Difficulty:** 4/10 **Prerequisites:** regions-celtic-ireland-03-instruments-voices-ii **Tags:** ireland, jig, reel, hornpipe, polka, slide, ornamentation, sean-nós, ballad, slow-air, lilting, session Overview If the instrument lessons taught you *who* speaks in an Irish session, this lesson teaches you *what language they speak*. Irish traditional music is organised around **dance forms** — reels, jigs, hornpipes, polkas, slides, and rarer metres — each with its own pulse, tempo range, and social history. Running alongside instrumental dance music is a parallel world of **song**: sean-nós in Irish, narrative ballads in English, drinking songs and laments, work songs and lilting. Ornamentation turns a skeleton tune into a recognisable regional accent; sets and variation turn a single melody into a living conversation. This lesson is long because the subject is wide. Take it in sections: learn to **identify the form** first (reel versus jig is the classic beginner trap), then study **ornament** on your own instrument, then explore **song traditions** as separate repertoires that sometimes share melodies with dance tunes. By the end you should be able to foot-tap confidently, name what you are hearing, and understand why a Clare polka set and a Donegal highland feel like different countries wearing the same passport. How to listen: metre, pulse, and feel Before memorising tune names, train your ear for **metre** (how beats are grouped) and **feel** (how those beats are articulated). Written time signatures are guides, not prisons: hornpipes may be notated in 4/4 but played with a dotted swing; sean-nós song may float across bar lines; slow airs may have almost no fixed beat at all. A useful habit: tap your foot and say the pulse aloud. Reels want a steady **ONE-two THREE-four** drive. Double jigs want **JIG-ged-y JIG-ged-y** — two main beats per bar, each divided into three. If you tap reel rhythm to a jig, experienced players will notice immediately and the tune will feel wrong in your body even if every note is correct. **Feel** also includes **lift** — the subtle emphasis that makes dance music bounce. Lift comes from bowing (fiddle), tonguing (flute, whistle), bellows pressure (accordion, concertina), or rhythmic articulation (banjo). It is not the same as playing louder; it is playing *with* the dance impulse, even when no one is dancing. ![Session musicians with bodhrán — pulse and lift in a live setting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/177-Bodhran-Hinnerk-Ruemenapf-0037-p70.jpg?width=640) Reels **Reels** are the workhorse of the Irish session. They are most often in **4/4** or notated in **2/2** (cut time) with a steady, driving pulse at moderate to fast tempo. A typical session might chain two or three reels before switching to jigs or hornpipes. Reels dominate because they suit the social energy of pub gatherings: forward motion, clear downbeats, room for melodic variation without losing the thread. Structurally, most reels are **binary** — an A part and a B part, each often eight bars, repeated. Musicians learn **parts** first, then **sets** of multiple tunes. Classic examples heard everywhere include *The Wind That Shakes the Barley*, *The Maid Behind the Bar*, *Drowsy Maggie*, *The Silver Spear*, and *The Musical Priest*. Diaspora fiddlers from Michael Coleman to Cape Breton players have spread reel repertoire so widely that the same tune may carry different ornaments in Sligo, Donegal, and New England. Reel bowing on fiddle often **slurs across beats** to create back-beat lift — a long bow stroke followed by a crisp catch. Flute and whistle players articulate with tonguing patterns that echo fiddle bowing. Banjo doubles the melody an octave higher with percussive attack. Accordion and concertina players phrase in bellows strokes that breathe with the tune. **Memorable detail:** Confusing a reel with a double jig is the most common beginner error. If the room starts tapping wrong, check the metre before blaming your instrument. Jigs: double, single, and slip Double jigs (6/8) **Double jigs** are in **6/8** time with a strong **two-beat** feel per bar: each beat divides into three eighth notes. They are the second most common session form after reels. Dance associations are broad — group céilí figures, solo step dance, and informal kitchen dancing all use jig rhythm. Famous double jigs include *The Swallowtail Jig*, *The Irish Washerwoman* (often played faster and lighter than newcomers expect), , *Banish Misfortune*, and *The Lilting Banshee*. The A and B parts repeat; musicians often pair a well-known jig with a lesser-known companion in a set. Single jigs **Single jigs** share 6/8 metre but lighten the rhythmic pattern — more crotchet–quaver (quarter–eighth) motion, less of the continuous triplet stream of a double jig. They are less common in modern sessions than doubles but appear in regional repertoire and older publications. Listen for a slightly **skipping** quality compared with the rolling drive of a double jig. If you transcribe a single jig from a recording, you may be tempted to write endless triplet groups because that is how double jigs look on the page. Resist: single-jig phrasing often **alternates** longer notes with quick catches, and fiddlers may bow the pattern differently from flute players' tonguing. *The Frost Is All Over* and *The Hag at the Churn* are often played with single-jig feel in some regions — always verify against a local source rather than a generic tune book. Single jigs also appear in **step-dance** teaching as **light jigs** — the same metre family with a pedagogical name. Musicians backing beginners learn that "jig" in a dance class may mean single-jig articulation even when the session next door plays doubles at full tilt. Slip jigs (9/8) **Slip jigs** use **9/8** — three beats per bar, each divided into three eighth notes. They feel **lighter and more asymmetrical** than double jigs, with a graceful lilt often linked to **soft-shoe** step dance in the competitive tradition. *Hardiman the Fiddler*, *The Butterfly*, and *The Foxhunter's Jig* are slip-jig standards. Slip jigs reward patience: the nine-beat bar can feel like it "turns" in the middle if you are used to six-beat jigs. Dancers and musicians share vocabulary here — slip-jig steps match the tune's elongated phrase shapes. ![Irish jig dance illustration, late 19th century — jig rhythm on the floor and in the tune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Irish_Jig%2C_from_National_Dances_%28N225%2C_Type_2%29_issued_by_Kinney_Bros._MET_DPB874573.jpg?width=640) Hornpipes **Hornpipes** are usually notated in **4/4** but played with a **dotted**, long-short **bounce** — slower than reels, with a swagger sometimes linked to sailor tunes and stage hornpipe dances. Names like *Off to California*, *The Sailor's Hornpipe*, *The Boys of Bluehill*, and *The Harvest Home* signal the type immediately to experienced players. Regional dotting varies: **Donegal** fiddlers and **Clare** players may articulate hornpipes differently. Some sessions play hornpipes relatively straight; others lean heavily into the dotted snap. Compare recordings rather than trusting a single metronome marking. Hornpipes suit **hard-shoe** step dance in competition — the dotted rhythm matches heel-and-toe percussion on the floor. Musicians accompanying feiseanna learn hornpipe tempo as a distinct category from session reels. Polkas Irish **polkas** are in **2/4** with a brisk, simple harmonic motion — not to be confused with Central European classical polkas or Oktoberfest clichés. They are strongest in **Munster**, especially **Sliabh Luachra** (the Cork–Kerry border region) and west Kerry. Polkas often appear in **sets** alternating with slides; dancers in set-dancing revival scenes depend on them. Examples include *Denis Murphy's Polka*, *Johnny I Hardly Knew Ye* (as instru

title: Irish Dance and Rhythm
snippet: Irish Dance and Rhythm Irish Dance and Rhythm **Track:** regions | **Tier:** 5 | **Difficulty:** 4/10 **Prerequisites:** regions-celtic-ireland-04-genres-forms **Tags:** ireland, dance, ceili, set-dance, stepdance, sean-nós, riverdance, fleadh, feis, rhythm Overview Irish dance a
text: Irish Dance and Rhythm Irish Dance and Rhythm **Track:** regions | **Tier:** 5 | **Difficulty:** 4/10 **Prerequisites:** regions-celtic-ireland-04-genres-forms **Tags:** ireland, dance, ceili, set-dance, stepdance, sean-nós, riverdance, fleadh, feis, rhythm Overview Irish dance and Irish traditional music grew up together — not as separate art forms that later collaborated, but as a single social technology for marking time, building community, and carrying identity. A reel in the session is not abstract metre; it is the same pulse that once drove figures in a farmhouse kitchen and still drives sixteen people through *The Siege of Ennis* in a parish hall. A hornpipe's dotted bounce is the sound hard-shoe dancers hear in their heels. This lesson maps **dance traditions** from the travelling masters of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries to the global spectacle of **Riverdance**, from improvised **sean-nós** on a half-door to adjudicated **feiseanna** where tempo arguments ruin friendships. Musicians need this map. You cannot play well for dancers if you do not know which beat is strong, which tradition you are serving, and why a set dancer's polka is not a session reel with the same name. Travelling dance masters (17th–18th centuries) Before competitions, before Comhaltas syllabi, before YouTube tutorials, **dance masters** (*máistir rince*) travelled from village to village teaching steps, posture, and figures. Sources from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries describe them as colourful figures — sometimes lodging with prosperous farmers, teaching in kitchens and barns, carrying canes or sticks to correct foot placement, and competing with rivals for pupils and prestige. Dance masters codified **regional repertoires** of steps while also spreading **shared figures** across counties. They linked **music and movement** explicitly: pupils learned to recognise jig from reel, to enter on the right beat, and to finish a figure cleanly so the musician could start the next tune. Oral histories describe masters who also **lilted** tunes or played fiddle — blurring the musician–dancer line that modern stage culture sometimes hardens. The master tradition declined with emigration, rural change, and the rise of organised classes, but its ghost survives in **step vocabulary**, **set figures**, and the cultural memory of dance as **portable skill** — something you could learn in one parish and carry to Boston or Birmingham. What masters taught Accounts from folklore collectors describe curricula that mixed **etiquette** and **athletics**: where to stand in a kitchen set, how to honour the musician, how to recover from a missed step without stopping the figure. Masters sometimes settled disputes between families over **who danced first** — dance was social power, not only entertainment. Rivals competed for pupils; legends tell of **dance-offs** on table tops and wagers on who could execute the most complex treble. Whether every story is literal truth matters less than what they reveal: dance mastery was **public reputation**, like fiddle virtuosity today. From kitchen to classroom By the early twentieth century, **Gaelic League** halls, **national schools**, and **church halls** replaced the itinerant master with **certified teachers**. An Coimisiún (1930) and later organisations standardised step syllabi. Set and céilí dancing were taught for **national revival** as well as fun — feet became evidence of cultural continuity. The travelling master did not vanish so much as **transform** into the weekly class, the summer school instructor, and the YouTube channel — but the pedagogical insight remains: dance is learned **in community**, not only from a screen. **Memorable detail:** Some accounts claim dance masters taught on **platforms** or **doors** to protect floors and amplify sound — a direct ancestor of sean-nós dance on a half-door. ![Historical Irish jig illustration — dance and music shared a social world long before stage shows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Irish_Jig%2C_from_National_Dances_%28N225%2C_Type_2%29_issued_by_Kinney_Bros._MET_DPB874573.jpg?width=640) Social dance: three broad families Irish dance today is not one style but a **family of traditions**: | Tradition | Scale | Footwork | Typical music | |-----------|-------|----------|---------------| | Céilí | Groups, choreographed figures | Moderate | Reels, jigs; céilí bands | | Set dancing | Four couples per set, quadrille heritage | Moderate, figure-driven | Reels, jigs, polkas, slides | | Step dance | Solo (or line spectacle) | Rapid, codified | Reels, jigs, hornpipes, slip jigs | | Sean-nós dance | Solo, improvisatory | Low, percussive | Sean-nós song, free rhythm | These overlap in musicians' lives — the same fiddler may play for a céilí, a set, and a pub session on one weekend — but each tradition asks different questions about **tempo**, **phrasing**, and **who leads** (caller, adjudicator, or singer). Céilí dancing **Céilí dancing** (*céilí* = social gathering) is **group choreography** for two to sixteen dancers, learned in classes and danced at weddings, festivals, and competitions. Footwork is **simpler** than solo step dance; emphasis falls on **formations** — circles, lines, chains, swings — and on moving together without collisions. Figures and repertoire Dances such as **The Siege of Ennis**, **The Walls of Limerick**, **The High Caul Cap**, **The Sweets of May**, and **The Fairy Reel** appear in repertoires worldwide thanks to Comhaltas teaching networks and diaspora classes. Each dance has a **prescribed figure sequence**: advance and retire, house, swing, basket, lead around. Musicians must hold **steady tempo** through long figures; dancers depend on predictable eight-bar phrasing. **The Siege of Ennis** — named for the Clare town — is the céilí dance many beginners learn first. Its figures teach basic skills used across the repertoire: facing partners, progressing around the set, and recovering when someone turns the wrong way (inevitable, human, forgiven). Céilí bands **Céilí bands** emerged in the twentieth century to provide **loud, steady** dance music — fiddle, flute, accordion, piano, drums, sometimes banjo — with clear downbeats for learners. They differ from pub sessions in **arrangement** and **volume**: less individual ornament, more ensemble drive. Bill McCabe, the Tulla Céilí Band, and Kilfenora Céilí Band names anchor the tradition on recordings. Céilí band rhythm can feel **straight** to session players — that is intentional. The job is to keep thirty beginners aligned, not to showcase personal rolls. Learning céilí as a musician If you are hired for a céilí night, expect **long tunes** — the same reel repeated through multiple figures without the session habit of switching every two minutes. Practice **endurance** at moderate tempo. Pianists and drummers in céilí bands anchor harmony and downbeat; melody players should avoid **over-ornamenting** when dancers are learning. **Ceili house** culture in diaspora cities (London, Boston, Sydney) kept figures alive when rural Ireland depopulated. Musicians in those scenes often know *Siege of Ennis* call patterns by heart — useful survival skill when a wedding floor fills unexpectedly. ![Fleadh Cheoil accordion band — ensemble drive for dancers and competition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/IMG_E9670_Holy_Cross_Accordion_Band_Atticall.jpg?width=640) Set dancing: quadrilles, Clare sets, and the 1980s revival adapts **French quadrille** figures to local taste — four couples facing in a square, dancing **figures** to matched tunes. Sets arrived in Ireland in the nineteenth century through military and gentry ballrooms, then **folk-processed** into regional variants with Irish tune choices and social contexts far from Parisian salons. Regional sets **Clare** is set-dancing heartland: **Corofin Plain Set**, **Cullaun Set**, **Clare Lancers**, and dozens of local names. **South Galwa

title: History, Revival, and Transmission
snippet: History, Revival, and Transmission History, Revival, and Transmission **Track:** regions | **Tier:** 6 | **Difficulty:** 5/10 **Prerequisites:** regions-celtic-ireland-05-dance **Tags:** ireland, revival, collectors, diaspora, transmission, fleadh, annals, 78rpm Overview Why does
text: History, Revival, and Transmission History, Revival, and Transmission **Track:** regions | **Tier:** 6 | **Difficulty:** 5/10 **Prerequisites:** regions-celtic-ireland-05-dance **Tags:** ireland, revival, collectors, diaspora, transmission, fleadh, annals, 78rpm Overview Why does one fiddle tune have four names, three keys, and two conflicting stories about who wrote it? Because Irish traditional music survived colonisation, famine, emigration, and language shift through **oral transmission** — and every link in that chain left fingerprints. A hearth version became a dancing master's version; a harper's air became a collector's manuscript; a Sligo fiddler's New York 78 became the "correct" way to play the tune back in Ireland. This lesson follows the music as far back as the sources allow: medieval annals and hymns, harp patronage and its collapse, travelling fiddlers and pipers, print collectors and police chiefs, diaspora shellac and radio revival, Comhaltas competitions and summer schools, archives and UNESCO — ending with the debate every living tradition faces: **competition clarity versus session swing**, **video access versus regional accent**, **innovation versus source**. You have met tune types, instruments, and dance forms in earlier tiers. Here you learn **how the repertoire moved** — and why understanding transmission makes you a better musician, not only a better historian. The annals: musicians in medieval Ireland Long before reels and polkas, Irish annalists recorded musicians as figures of skill and status. Wikipedia's *Music of Ireland* article draws on the **Irish annals** to list native musicians from the High and Late Medieval eras — harpers, **tiompanists** (players of the tiompan), singers, and craftsmen who built instruments. These entries are not session reports; they are obituaries and notices that treat music as high craft tied to churches, courts, and learned families. A chronological sample (dates as given in the annals): | Date | Figure | Role | |------|--------|------| | **921 BC** | Cú Congalta, priest of Lann-Leire | *Tethra* (singer or orator) for voice, personal form and knowledge | | **1011** | Connmhach Ua Tomhrair | Priest and chief singer of Cluain-mic-Nois | | **1168** | Amhlaeibh Mac Innaighneorach | Chief **ollamh** of Ireland in **harp-playing** | | **1226** | **Aed mac Donn Ó Sochlachain** | Erenagh of Cong; eminent for chanting, tuning harps, and making an instrument none had made before; also poetry, engraving, writing | | **1269** | Aed Ó Finn | Master of music and minstrelsy | | **1329** | Maol Ruanaidh Cam Ó Cearbhaill | **Tiompanist**, murdered in the Braganstown Massacre, County Louth | | **1330** | Mael Sechlainn Mac Carmaic | General entertainer | | **1343** | Donnchad Clereach Ó Maol Braonáin | Choral canon of Elphin, killed by an arrow | | **1357** | Donn Shléibhe Mac Cerbaill | Accomplished musician | | **1360** | Gilla na Naem Ó Conmaigh | Music ollamh of Thomond | | **1361** | Magraith Ó Fionnachta | Chief musician and tiompanist to the Síol Muireadaigh | | **1364** | Bran Ó Brain | Skilful tympanist | | **1369** | John Mac Egan, Gilbert Ó Bardan | Accomplished young harpers of Conmaicne | | **1469** | Ruaidrí mac Donnchad Ó Dálaigh | "The most musical-handed harpist in all Ireland" | | **1490** | Diarmait MacCairbre | Harper, executed | | **1553** | Tadhg, son of Ruaidhri Ó Comhdhain | Ollamh of Éire and Alba in music | | **1561** | Naisse mac Cithruadh | Drowned on Lough Gill | | **1589** | Daighre Ó Duibhgeannáin | "A most affable, musical man" | Read the list as evidence of **institutional music** — church singers, court harpers, hereditary learned families — not as a direct pipeline to today's pub session. Still, the thread is continuous: Ireland documented musicians as culturally central long before tourism boards existed. ![Sixteenth-century Irish warpipes player](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Rosgall.jpg?width=640) Early poetry, hymns, and song roots Medieval and early modern **Irish poetry** often blurred verse and music. Surviving **airs** are scarce before 1700 — Wikipedia's *Irish music collecting* article notes how little composed Irish music from that era survives — but literary texts and later transcriptions preserve a song world that fed the slow-air and sean-nós streams. **Rop tú mo baile** (*Be Thou My Vision*) — a sixth-century hymn attributed to **Dallán Forgaill** — was published in English in **1905** by **Mary Elizabeth Byrne** and is widely sung today in churches and folk settings. It exemplifies how early Irish sacred verse re-enters modern repertoire through scholarly translation and arrangement. **The Blackbird of Belfast Lough** (*Int én bec* / *An t-éan beag*) — a medieval Irish lyric — has been translated by poets including **Seamus Heaney**, **Ciaran Carson**, and **Frank O'Connor**, and recorded in modern interpretations (e.g. Pádraigín Ní Uallacháin's *Songs of the Scribe*, choral work by **Anúna**, projects by Caitríona O'Leary). Such pieces connect "ancient Ireland" to living performance — not as museum pieces but as material contemporary artists re-voice. Collectors from the eighteenth century onward gathered Carolan compositions, bardic remnants, and popular airs into print. **John and William Neale's** *A Collection of the Most Celebrated Irish Tunes* (**1724**, Dublin) is the first recorded collection of Irish traditional music; the surviving copy is associated with **Edward Bunting** at Queen's University Belfast. **John Playford's** *The Dancing Master* (mid-seventeenth century) and **Durfey's** *Pills to Purge Melancholy* (late seventeenth century) already carried Irish tunes into British print culture — evidence of cross-channel exchange before the famine diaspora. Irish musicians abroad — early medieval to early modern Irish musical skill travelled with monks, scholars, and exiles long before the nineteenth-century steamship. - **Cú Chuimne** (died **747**) spent much of his life in Gaelic Scotland and composed at least one hymn. - **Foillan** (seventh century) travelled Britain and France; around **653** he taught **psalmody** to nuns at Nievelle at the request of Saint Gertrude of Brabant. - **Tuotilo** (c. **850**–c. **915**), active in Italy and Germany, was noted as musician and composer. - **Helias of Cologne** (died **1040**) is held to have introduced **Roman chant** to Cologne. - **Aaron Scotus** (died **18 November 1052**) was an acclaimed composer of **Gregorian chant** in Germany. - **Donell Dubh Ó Cathail** (c. 1560s–c. 1660) served as musician to **Viscount Buttevant** and, with his uncle **Donell Óge Ó Cathail**, as **harper to Elizabeth I**. This pattern — Irish performers valued on European stages — prefigures the Chicago fiddle studio and the Riverdance arena. Diaspora is not only loss; it is also **export of expertise**. Harp patronage, Carolan, and the Belfast festival Until the seventeenth century, **harpers** were patronised by the aristocracy in Ireland. That Gaelic patronage system collapsed with **Gaelic Ireland** in the eighteenth century; the hereditary harp tradition dwindled toward extinction. **Turlough Carolan** (1670–1738) is the best-known harper-composer of the transition era. Blind from youth, he travelled Ireland composing **planxties** and other pieces for patrons — over **200 compositions** are known. His music blends native melody with elements of contemporary **baroque** taste; tunes like *Planxty Irwin* and *Carolan's Farewell to Music* entered the folk repertoire and are still played on fiddle, flute, and harp. **John Lee** published a collection of his compositions in **1780**; **Joseph Cooper Walker** included Carolan tunes in *Historical Memoirs of the Irish Bards* (**1786**). By **1792**, few traditional harpers remained. The **Belfast Harp Festival** (11–14 July **1792**), organised by Dr. James McDonnell, Robert Bradshaw, and Henry Joy McCracken in the **Assembly Rooms, Belfast**, gat

title: Representative Fusions and Scenes
snippet: Representative Fusions and Scenes Representative Fusions and Scenes **Track:** regions | **Tier:** 7 | **Difficulty:** 6/10 **Prerequisites:** regions-celtic-ireland-06-history **Tags:** ireland, fusion, celtic-rock, showband, diaspora, riverdance, folk-revival, celtic-punk Overv
text: Representative Fusions and Scenes Representative Fusions and Scenes **Track:** regions | **Tier:** 7 | **Difficulty:** 6/10 **Prerequisites:** regions-celtic-ireland-06-history **Tags:** ireland, fusion, celtic-rock, showband, diaspora, riverdance, folk-revival, celtic-punk Overview This lesson maps **how Irish traditional music left the kitchen, the pub session, and the fleadh stage** to meet ballroom crowds, American television, rock amplifiers, jazz harmony, New Age production, Broadway spectacle, and diaspora cities on three continents. It assumes you already know the collectors, Comhaltas, and transmission story from the history lesson — here the focus is **named bands, fusion genres, and scenes** from the 1950s to the present. Think of Irish music as a tree with many branches, not a single "authentic" trunk. Showbands taught a generation stagecraft; the Clancy Brothers dressed trad for Ed Sullivan; Horslips plugged harps into Marshall stacks; Planxty made the bouzouki a session standard; The Pogues poured Guinness into punk; Riverdance sold step dance to stadiums; Chicago kept O'Neill's tune books alive. Each branch fed back into the others — session players learn from punk albums; metal bands quote slip jigs; country singers cover sean-nós melodies in English. **Memorable detail:** Almost every fusion act on this list contains at least one musician who also plays straight trad — the boundary is porous, not a wall. --- 1. Irish Showbands (1950s–1970s) Formation and scene **Irish showbands** emerged in the late 1950s as the social centre of rural and small-town Ireland shifted to **ballrooms and dance halls** — purpose-built venues and converted cinemas where young people courted, drank, and danced on Saturday nights. Before discos, before television dominated entertainment, the showband was the **house band of a nation on the move**: electrified, horn-led, dressed in matching suits, playing six nights a week on a circuit from Donegal to Kerry. A typical lineup ran **vocals, electric guitar, bass, drums, saxophone, trumpet or trombone, and keyboards** — sometimes two saxes. Repertoire mixed **chart covers** (Beatles, Motown, country hits), **céilí sets** for the older crowd, and **showmanship**: coordinated steps, comedy patter, costume changes. Bands travelled in vans with their own PA, competing for residency slots at halls like the **Galway Bay Hotel**, the **Crystal Ballroom** in Bundoran, and hundreds of parish halls. Key acts and members Hundreds of bands existed; a few became national names: | Band | Notes | |------|-------| | **The Royal Showband** (Waterford) | Brendan Bowyer — often cited as the first superstar showband vocalist | | **The Capitol Showband** | Featured **Des Lee** and later **Butch Moore** (Eurovision 1965) | | **The Miami Showband** | Cross-border lineup; tragically attacked in 1975 — a wound in the Troubles era | | **Drifters Showband** | Brendan Bowyer after leaving the Royal | | **The Freshmen** | Harmonic sophistication; Billy Brown arrangements | Individual musicians rotated between bands the way jazz sidemen did — **learning repertoire breadth and stage presence** that would later surface in folk-rock and country-and-Irish careers. Musical approach Showbands were **dance functional first**: four-to-the-floor rhythms, singalong choruses, medleys to keep feet moving. Horn sections voiced country and soul hits; guitarists learned **country picking** from American records. When a band dropped a reel or polka set, it was usually **simplified and amplified** — not the ornamented session version, but recognisable to dancers who had grown up with ceili bands. The showband era coincided with **rural electrification and rising car ownership** — teenagers could reach a hall twenty miles away. Radio programmes like **RTÉ's Showband Show** (from 1965) broadcast performances into kitchens, creating national hits overnight. Landmark moments - **Brendan Bowyer** and — showband dance crazes - **Butch Moore**, *Walking the Streets in the Rain* — Ireland's first Eurovision entry (1965) - The **Miami Showband massacre** (1975) — political violence intersecting entertainment (not musical legacy, but historical context) Legacy By the late 1970s, **discos, cover bands in hotels, and television** eroded the circuit. Yet showbands matter for trad students because they: 1. **Kept dance music socially central** through a period when pure trad was unfashionable in urban media 2. **Trained musicians** in reading charts, blending, and working crowds — skills Planxty and Moving Hearts would exploit 3. **Bridged American country and Irish melody** — direct ancestor of country-and-Irish **Memorable detail:** Many future trad and rock players started in showbands; the ballroom was Ireland's conservatoire of popular musicianship. ![St Malachy's dance hall, Edendork — built in the showband era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/St_Malachy's_dance_hall,_Edendork_-_geograph.org.uk_-_259005.jpg?width=640) --- 2. Country-and-Irish Formation and context **Country-and-Irish** (also **country 'n' Irish** or **Irish country**) fuses **American country music** — pedal steel, Nashville song structure, close harmony — with **Irish ballad melody, fiddle ornament, and themes of emigration, farming, and family**. It is not "trad" in the Comhaltas sense, but it is **deeply Irish popular music**: sung in English (sometimes Irish phrases), sold in record shops from Letterkenny to Limerick, and performed at **cabaret lounges, festivals, and RTÉ television**. The genre rose as showbands declined and **rural audiences aged into country tastes** shaped by American radio, emigrant letters, and records brought home from Birmingham or Boston. Big Tom and The Mainliners **Formation:** **Tom McBride** ("Big Tom", 1936–2018) from **Castleblayney, County Monaghan**, formed **The Mainliners** in 1966 with guitarist **Seamus McMahon**, saxophonist **Henry McMahon**, drummer **Ronnie Duffy**, bassist **Ginger Morgan**, trombonist **Cyril McKevitt**, and keyboardist **John Beattie**. They were a **showband-turned-country** outfit — not pure Nashville, but horn-backed country ballads with Irish emotional directness. **Musical approach:** Warm baritone vocals, sentimental lyrics, fiddle and steel colouring Irish step and waltz rhythms. (1966), performed on **The Showband Show**, became a defining hit — mothers wept; sales soared. Songs like **"Four Country Roads"** and **"Back to Castleblayney"** rooted identity in place. **Landmark albums/songs:** , *Four Country Roads*, *Old Love Letters*; decades of studio albums and ballroom tours. **Legacy:** Big Tom was inaugural inductee to the **Irish Country Music Awards Hall of Fame** (2016). A bronze statue stands on Muckno Street, Castleblayney (unveiled 2018). He proved country-and-Irish could sustain a **forty-year career** without American stardom — domestic fame at stadium scale. Daniel O'Donnell **Formation:** **Daniel O'Donnell** (born 1961, Kincasslagh, Donegal) began professionally in the 1980s, building a career distinct from Big Tom's brassy showband roots — **softer, crooner-led, television-friendly**. **Musical approach:** Clean production, romantic and nostalgic lyrics, occasional Irish-language songs, duets with **Mary Duff** and others. Less honky-tonk than Big Tom; more **middle-of-the-road country pop** with Irish accent and fiddle fills. **Landmark work:** Albums such as *I Need You* and relentless touring schedule (often cited among the busiest live acts in Europe); **BBC television specials** brought him British audiences beyond the Irish diaspora. **Legacy:** Country-and-Irish's **second-generation star** — proof the genre outlived its ballroom origins. For trad musicians, O'Donnell represents the **parallel radio universe** many rural listeners inhabit; knowing his audience helps teachers connect with students whose first Irish music was country, not sean-nós. **Memorable detail:** Big Tom and Daniel

snippet: Irish Tunes — Forms, History, and Recordings Irish Tunes — Forms, History, and Recordings **Track:** regions | **Tier:** 4.5 | **Difficulty:** 5/10 **Prerequisites:** regions-celtic-ireland-04-genres-forms **Tags:** ireland, tunes, reel, jig, hornpipe, recordings Overview This le
text: Irish Tunes — Forms, History, and Recordings Irish Tunes — Forms, History, and Recordings **Track:** regions | **Tier:** 4.5 | **Difficulty:** 5/10 **Prerequisites:** regions-celtic-ireland-04-genres-forms **Tags:** ireland, tunes, reel, jig, hornpipe, recordings Overview This lesson turns the tune-type field guide into **named repertoire**. You will meet representative reels, jigs, hornpipes, polkas, slides, slow airs, and a planxty — with oldest references, players who popularised each tune, regional variants, and multiple YouTube examples in different styles. Listen comparatively: the same title can sound like a Sligo roll-heavy reel in one hands and a spare Donegal reading in another. That variation is the tradition working. The Silver Spear The Silver Spear is among the most played reels in sessions worldwide. Francis O'Neill included it in *Music of Ireland*; Michael Coleman's New York 78s helped fix a setting that many players still treat as a reference. Martin Hayes and other Clare fiddlers often approach the tune with more space and dynamic breathing. Compare recordings below — notice bowing, ornament density, and tempo relative to dance. The Kesh Jig appears in Brendan Breathnach's *Ceol Rince na hÉireann* and has become a learner's gateway into 6/8 repertoire. It chains easily with *The Merry Blacksmith* and other D-major jigs in pub sets. More session standards | Tune | Form | Note | |------|------|------| | *The Wind That Shakes the Barley* | Reel | Political associations; many settings | | *Drowsy Maggie* | Reel | High-energy session opener | | *The Butterfly* | Slip jig | 9/8 asymmetry; graceful step | | *Off to California* | Hornpipe | Dotted bounce; emigration theme | | *Sí Bheag Sí Mhór* | Planxty | Carolan harp piece adapted widely | Use **Play all** at the top to hear curated examples, or tap ▶ beside each player row. The Silver Spear Michael Coleman New York recordings fixed settings still played today. Sligo fiddler whose 78s popularised many session standards Martin Hayes Reinterprets standards with slow intros and dynamic range. Contemporary Clare fiddler with breathing phrasing Tune names and settings vary by region and collector. Reels, jigs, hornpipes, and polkas each have distinct metre. 78s and archives document how standards crystallised. Compare two recordings to hear regional bowing and ornament. Session sets chain tunes of the same form before switching.
